name: Finding the Number of Days Above the Average Temperature
description: Construct a program that reads a series of temperatures and reports the average temperature and the number of the days that are above the average. Assume that the input values could have a decimal point.

comments.content: We need to first ask the user how many days of temperature data will be provided. To read the input value from user, we need to define a Scanner object. We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.
We prompt the user to enter how many days of temperature data will be provided.
We need to read the number of days that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the input integer by calling the nextInt() method because this input is an integer.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.

We first need to define an array referred by variable temps for storing the temperatures that the user provides. This statement declares an array variable, temps, creates a double array with a length of numDays, and assigns its reference to temps. By default, each number in the array is 0.0. We will later update the array elements with the temperature values that we receive from the user. We need this array later to iterate over the temperature values and calculate the number of the days that are above the average.
We need variable total to maintain a running total, which means the sum of the temperature values that the user has entered so far. Of course, the total should be initialized with 0.

We want to read each temperature value and calculate the running total for the temperature values that the user has entered so far.

We also need to add each temperature value in the array to later count the number of days that are above the average. Therefore, we use a for loop to iterate over the array indexes and add a temperature value to each index.

We need the array indexes to have a length of numDays and start at 0 with every integer number up to but not including numDays, where variable numDays is the number of days for which the user will provide the temperature values.

In the first part of the loop header, we define a control variable i and initialize it to 0. In the second part of the loop header, we test whether the control variable has reached the termination threshold. The loop is repeated if the control variable is less than numDays and terminates when the control variable reaches numDays. In the third part of the loop header, we increment the control variable by 1 after each iteration of the loop.

Note that the first part is executed once before the loop starts, the second part is executed before each iteration, and the third part is executed after each iteration of the loop. Also note that the increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable i and the result is stored back into the variable i. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement i = i + 1.
We prompt the user to enter the temperature values.

We want to store the temperature value that the user has entered in the array temps. We read the value by calling nextDouble() method because temperature could have a decimal point. We assign this double to the element at index i of the array.
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid double value.

We need to add each value read to the running total that is stored in variable total. So, in each iteration, we add the value read (which we stored is the index i of the array) in the array to the variable total and store the result back into the variable total.

The += operator adds the value of the element at the index i of the array to the value of the variable total and the result is stored in the variable total. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement total = total + temps[i].
We close the scanner as we do not want to process any input from the user in the rest of the program.
We need variable average to store the average of the temperature values that the user has entered. We declare it as double because average could be a floating-point number.
We need the if statement before computing the average to avoid a divide-by-zero error. This occurs if the user enters 0 for the number of days.
If the user enters 0 for the number of days, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints the text "No temperature values were entered." to the default standard output stream. This text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

If the first test fails (i.e., when the user enters a positive number greater than zero for the number of days), then the body of the previous if statement will not be executed, instead the body of this else statement will be executed.

We need to compute the average by dividing the sum of the temperature values by the number of the days that we received their temperature values. Notice that both variables in the division are int and dividing an int by an int results in an int. Since we want to keep the fractional part, we need to cast one of the operands to a floating point data type like double.

When floating point value total is divided by an integer value numDays, the value of numDays is promoted to a floating point value automatically, before the division takes place, producing a floating point result.
We need variable above to count how many temperature values were above average. Of course, it should be initialized with 0 because we have not started counting yet.

We want to iterate over the array temps and count the number of temperature values that are above the average. We traverse the array elements using for–each statement. This for loop assigns the name x to each of the elements in the array in turn, from left to right, and the statements in the loop body will be executed for each.

We need to compare the array element that we visited with the average of temperature values stored in variable average. If that value is greater than the average, then we need to increase the number of days above average by 1.
If visited value in the array is greater than the average, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
When the current temperature value is greater than the average, then we have to increment the number of days above the average by 1.
The increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable above and the result is stored back into the variable above. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement above = above + 1.
This statement concatenates the given text and value of variable average and prints the result of concatenation. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

Note that we concatenate the content of two strings using the + operator. Also, note that the concatenating and printing are done in the same line. That is, we don't have to store the concatenated string to a new variable at first and then print it in the next line.
This statement concatenates the value of variable above and the given text and prints the result of concatenation. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

Note that we concatenate the content of two strings using the + operator. Also, note that the concatenating and printing are done in the same line. That is, we don't have to store the concatenated string to a new variable at first and then print it in the next line.
